IBOGAINE KILLER

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A controversial rehab drug administered by a dentist claimed the life of a Canadian citizen in Durban – we investigate.

Unique Selling Point:
EXCLUSIVE FOOTAGE OF THE DEATH
A DENTIST MASQUERADING AS A DENTIST
HEARTBREAKING INTERVIEWS
RECORDING OF THE DENTIST ADMITTING GUILT TO THE WIDOW
QUESTIONS ABOUT OUR THE EFFICIENCY OF OUR LEGAL SYSTEM FROM INTERNATIONAL VICTIMS



Summary:

Ibogaine is a highly controversial drug only available in 7 countries – South Africa is one of them. Intended to treat opiod addiction, but not recommended for benzodiazepines.

A Canadian citizen came to SA to get off his anti-depressant addiction. He arrived and died two days later at a rehab centre run by not a doctor but a dentist.

The family fears that the South African legal system will fail serve justice for what they say is the murder of Milos Martinovic.

We get exclusive interviews with his wife and father – both broken by his loss, angry at charlatan dentist and deeply concerned about the rule of law in the country.

Further information:
IBOGAINE
The controversial drug ibogaine promises a relatively fast, relatively easy way of beating heroin or cocaine addiction. The active ingredient of the root bark of the African shrub Tabernanthe iboga, that originates in Gabon, Africa.

Ibogaine is not a new drug, and a substantial amount of research has been done on it. It’s seems to inhabit a space on the frontiers of science – it may turn out to be effective, and alternatively, it may turn out to be very dangerous. The kind of randomised clinical studies in humans that can give definitive answers to these questions has, however, not yet been done. Some literature warns that ibogaine is not to be used for the treatment of abuse of antidepressants and anti-anxiety drugs, OxyContin and morphine, as it states that this can result in respiratory arrest and heart failure.

Ibogaine is outlawed in some countries, owing to a lack of research. What research there is on ibogaine apparently suggests that it should not be used for the treatment of abuse of antidepressants and anti-anxiety drugs, OxyContin and morphine.

In South Africa it was declared a schedule 6 drug and as such could only be in possession of medical doctors to begin with. Ibogaine is illegal in USA, France, England and many other countries. SA is one of only 7 countries worldwide where the drug is “allowed”.

It is also important that when someone does decide to take ibogaine, it is done under experienced supervision. Without a formal medical network to refer to, determining the expertise of the person conducting the treatment may, however, be difficult.

ENTER ANWAR JEEWA & THE MINDS ALIVE REHAB CENTRE
Jeewa sells himself as a guru in ibogaine use and doctor even though his only qualification is a dentist. Jeewa is a self-confessed drug addict who boasts on the internet during an international seminar on the uses of ibogaine that he used every imaginable drug on the market.

According to the Minds Alive website, it says the facility has, since 2006, been the “leaders” in the field and had treated a “range of chemical dependencies, compulsive behaviours, depression and anxiety with the use of ibogaine therapy”.




JEEWA’s QUALIFICATIONS OR RATHER LACK THERE OF
Jeewa is - at best - a self-confessed dentist and not a medical doctor, permitted to prescribe, supervise or control the use of scheduled drugs such as the kind described.

He claims the clinic is “mostly a non-profit organisation” – yet he caters for international patients that are encourage to pay the fees in cash. Costs are between R20 000 – R26000 for a five day treatment plan.

CASE STUDY
In early November 2017, a 26-year-old Canadian man, Milos Martinovic, flew to South Africa to undergo treatment for his drug addiction.

He was addicted to prescription drugs after his mother’s death in August 2017. He (Martinovic) did his internet research on how to rid himself of prescription drugs dependency and came across Anwar Jeewa who is the owner of Minds Alive in Westville, Durban. Convinced that it was the solution – he booked the trip to South Africa.
He arrived on the 5th of November 2017 - two days after he was admitted to an unlicensed Durban facility, he was dead.

Martinovic died “on camera” (CCTV) – there was no monitoring as promised, the staff appear clueless and unable to do CPR. Jeewa doesn’t even attempt CPR, stands on his phone calling in paramedics who then arrive and attempt CPR.

His family is concerned about the way the case is being handled and are worried that justice may not be served – they fly out regularly to attend court appearances and have appointed a private investigator and attorney to investigate the case and ensure that justice be served.

THE CRIMNAL CASE
The nurse , Mrs. Zama, who was on duty on the night of Martinovic’s death as well as Anwar Jeewa has been arrested on charges of culpable homicide.

Jeewa has been released on bail and has handed his passport to police. As part of his bail conditions, He was ordered to report to his local police station twice weekly until his case was finalised. He was also ordered to cease operations at Minds Alive until his case was finalised or he was issued with a licence.

A post-mortem established that the Canadian had overdosed on Alprazolam (Xanax).
A toxicological report also showed levels of ibogaine. Should Milos have been checked for benzodiazepines and opiate levels, it would have alarmed the doctors to the levels present. Milos should then have been weaned off the benzodiazepines and opiates prior to the commencement of ibogaine treatment. Investigators believe Milos died as a result of poor screening, an incorrect diagnosis and the wrongful administration of ibogaine. It appeared that he was given ibogaine despite him being on Xanax, OxyContin and morphine.

The investigating officer is officially investigating a charge of murder as Martinovic’s death should have been foreseen (dolus eventualis – same as in Oscar Pretorius’s case)

MANUFACTURING & DISTRUBUTION
A police raid of Jeewa’s premises had turned up large quantities of “brown powder and bark-like powder, presumably ibogaine”, large amounts of ibogaine capsules, large amounts of schedule five and six prescription drugs, unscheduled drugs, illicit drugs and a pad of blank prescriptions which purported to have been signed by another doctor.

Jeewa is suspected of supplying the international ibogain trade with the drug. He sent the ibogaine to places such as Australia, USA, Spain, etc marking his parcels as “documents” – confirmed when his computers were confiscated during a police raid as well as his assitant. Since his arrest the court has ordered that he closes his rehabilitation centre but he merely refers or treats his patients in a rehab centre situated in Mauritius (he has an “interest” in the Mauritius centre)

INTERFERENCE WITH THE CASE
The Deputy Mayor in Durban has made “enquiries” on the progress of the investigation – the investigation officer was called in by his superiors and told to hand over a copy of the docket because it was requested by the Deputy Mayor.

ADDITIONAL FOOTAGE & RECORDINGS
There are numerous YouTube videos where either presents himself Jeewa or attends conferences presented by other ibogaine experts. Audio

POTENTIAL SECOND CASE STUDY
Minds Alive (Anwar Jeewa) also provided ibogaine to a rehabilitation centre in Rustenburg and during 2018 another patient there died after ibogain treatment. The family lives in Cape Town.

EXPERT
USA based doctor Deborah Mash working as a doctor in Miami was employed by the USA FDA to do research in ibogaine. She was featured in the 2006 story – and has agreed to another Skype Interview with us.

She is shocked and appalled by the misuse of Ibogaine. She will also testify in the case against Jeewa.

The most compelling scientific evidence for the use of ibogaine against drug addiction stems from animal studies. As long ago as 1991, studies found that ibogaine helped to diminish opioid self-administration in rats and to alleviate withdrawal symptoms.

Unfortunately, very few studies have been done in human subjects, and when they were done, they were done outside of traditional clinical settings. Yet, research conducted by Dr Deborah Mash, Professor of Neurology at the University of Miami, indicates that the use of the drug to treat opioid dependence in humans may be viable. Yet, until further trials, serious concerns about the safety and efficacy of ibogain will remain.

RESEARCH
"Serious toxic effects (in therapeutic doses) include: slowing of the heart, fall in blood pressure, heart failure, seizures, paralysis, and respiratory arrest (these toxic effects have been reported following therapy with ibogaine). Furthermore, "deaths (related to cardiac arrhythmia) have been reported in several individuals taking ibogaine. (There is, however, inadequate data to determine whether ibogaine may have been a primary factor in these cases.)"

And, despite extensive research, the exact mechanism of the drug is still not fully understood. "Ibogaine appears to have a novel mechanism of action that differs from other existing pharmacotherapies of addiction. "Ibogaine’s effects may result from complex interactions between multiple neurotransmitter systems rather than predominant activity within a single neurotransmitter system."

In the early 1990s the US Food and Drug Administration gave its approval for an ibogaine study in humans. Due to a lack of funds, this study never took place. The US National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) decided not to support such a study at a meeting in 1995.
With the kind of scientific studies that would give more clarity on the safety and efficacy of ibogaine not happening, the underground movement – a kind of a "medical subculture" related to ibogaine, gained momentum.

As Gerbus Muller, a toxicologist at the University of Stellenbosch, points out, "There is scant objective information on clinical efficacy, and clinical reports in scientific medical journals only cover a few dozen patients."

Press Release:


Ibogaine Death
Ibogaine is a highly controversial rehab drug which is intended mainly for the treatment of opioid addiction. It’s available in just six countries. Now a Durban-based dentist stands accused of killing a Canadian man, after he allegedly administered the drug to the addict and the victim’s family is demanding answers. Carte Blanche investigates.
Producer: Nicky Troll
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender
Watch the trailer

IBOGAINE SCRIPT

VO: When it comes to beating addiction, for drug addicts, any potential cure is worth a try – even controversial, experimental drugs.

Ibogaine originates from Gabon - the active ingredient found in the root bark of the Tabernanthe Iboga shrub. It is not a cure for drug addiction – instead, it is said to block withdrawal symptoms during a drug detox.

Ibogaine is only permitted in 6 countries globally - with very limited research available, it has not been approved by drug authorities in most countries.

It is even on offer in South Africa – despite, it being illegal .

LINK: Addicts are flocking to the country desperate for a solution – but because the treatment falls into largely unknown territory – the apparent cure is not without risk. OPENING

VO: Dr Deborah Mash spoke us via Skype from Miami – a Professor of neurology and of molecular and cellular pharmacology. As one of the world’s foremost experts on ibogaine – she is concerned about so-called underground treatment facilities.

DR MASH: they are not qualified, they are not skilled, they not may not even have a pure drug product. INT1 M4

VO: 26 year old Canadian Citizen, Milos Martinovic’s lost his mother to brain cancer in AUGUST 2017. Battling to cope, he turned to prescription meds and developed an addiction.

Desperate to get clean – in November that year - he decided on a treatment centre in South Africa, Minds Alive run by Dr Anwar Jeewa.

MAYBE UPSOUND FROM A CONFERENCE – beyond psychodellics

VO: Minds Alive claims to be leaders in ibogaine therapy and promise results in less than a week.

But just 6 hours after starting treatment, Milos Martinovic was not on the road to recovery – he was dead.

BROOKE: // it’s a pain that you could feel in your bones every inch of your body seeing your husband, the person you love more than life it self and seeing him not breathing// [crying] INT1 M16

VO: Devastated, Milos’ wife Brooke and his father Miki Martinovic flew to South Africa – things didn’t add up and they wanted answers.

BROOKE: I need to know exactly what happened if I am going to sleep at night. INT2 M2

VO: Milos was cross-addicted to Oxycontin – and Xanax – the one an opioid used for pain, the other a benzodiazepine that treats anxiety. He disclosed this to Dr Jeewa prior to arriving as well as on his screening form when he was admitted.

LINK: Intended to treat opioid addictions – Ibogaine is not recommended for treating benzodiazepines addictions. It seems that in Milos’ case a big – red – flag was most likely, ignored. IBOGAINE

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 28 June 2019 Press Release: Ibogaine Death Ibogaine is a highly controversial rehab drug which is intended mainly for the treatment of opioid addiction. It’s available in just six countries. Now a Durban-based dentist stands accused of killing a Canadian man, after he allegedly administered the drug to the addict and the victim’s family is demanding answers. Carte Blanche investigates. Producer: Nicky Troll Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender Watch the trailer Script: IBOGAINE SCRIPT VO: When it comes to beating addiction, for drug addicts, any potential cure is worth a try – even controversial, experimental drugs. Ibogaine originates from Gabon - the active ingredient found in the root bark of the Tabernanthe Iboga shrub. It is not a cure for drug addiction – instead, it is said to block withdrawal symptoms during a drug detox. Ibogaine is only permitted in 6 countries globally - with very limited research available, it has not been approved by drug authorities in most countries. It is even on offer in South Africa – despite, it being illegal . LINK: Addicts are flocking to the country desperate for a solution – but because the treatment falls into largely unknown territory – the apparent cure is not without risk. OPENING VO: Dr Deborah Mash spoke us via Skype from Miami – a Professor of neurology and of molecular and cellular pharmacology. As one of the world’s foremost experts on ibogaine – she is concerned about so-called underground treatment facilities. DR MASH: they are not qualified, they are not skilled, they not may not even have a pure drug product. INT1 M4 VO: 26 year old Canadian Citizen, Milos Martinovic’s lost his mother to brain cancer in AUGUST 2017. Battling to cope, he turned to prescription meds and developed an addiction. Desperate to get clean – in November that year - he decided on a treatment centre in South Africa, Minds Alive run by Dr Anwar Jeewa. MAYBE UPSOUND FROM A CONFERENCE – beyond psychodellics VO: Minds Alive claims to be leaders in ibogaine therapy and promise results in less than a week. But just 6 hours after starting treatment, Milos Martinovic was not on the road to recovery – he was dead. BROOKE: // it’s a pain that you could feel in your bones every inch of your body seeing your husband, the person you love more than life it self and seeing him not breathing// [crying] INT1 M16 VO: Devastated, Milos’ wife Brooke and his father Miki Martinovic flew to South Africa – things didn’t add up and they wanted answers. BROOKE: I need to know exactly what happened if I am going to sleep at night. INT2 M2 VO: Milos was cross-addicted to Oxycontin – and Xanax – the one an opioid used for pain, the other a benzodiazepine that treats anxiety. He disclosed this to Dr Jeewa prior to arriving as well as on his screening form when he was admitted. LINK: Intended to treat opioid addictions – Ibogaine is not recommended for treating benzodiazepines addictions. It seems that in Milos’ case a big – red – flag was most likely, ignored. IBOGAINE VO: Minds Alive knew he had the pills on him and did not confiscate it – instead, he was allowed to continue self-medicating. BROOKE: I was told that the second he got there he would be searched everything would be taken and that the medical staff who were employed there would be the ones administrating the medication. // none of those things had happened. INT1 M11 VO: Dr Mash is adamant that self-medication at a rehab facility is highly irregular. DR MASH: ibogaine gets converted to an active metabolite, // if this man was already at risk for a toxic reaction – and then you’re giving more ibogaine over that time – that caused the death. INT1 M17 VO: Dr Anwar Jeewa is facing criminal charges , but agreed to be interviewed . ONLY TREAT BENZO’s D – listen to yourself – addict, come here A – correct A – yah so – what is wrong D – I tell you what is wrong he is dead MIKI: After a year and a half we are still struggling, // what we can do nothing – how to prove to this government it was his mistake - he kill my son. INT1 M17 VO: The family appointed Durban Private Investigator, Marius Booysen, to help drive the investigation. The discoveries so far have been shocking. MARIUS: Minds Alive is not a registered rehab centre. Anwar Jeewa is not a doctor, he is not qualified to treat people. INT4 M29 VO: Anwar Jeewa is a non-practising dentist . On the Minds Alive website – Dr Jeewa – is the only doctor listed . He holds an Honours degree in Religion and Social Transformation and a Masters degree in Social Science. D – not a qualified doctor A – correct 09.48.40 D – dentists A – no I wasn’t I acting as a medical doctor – nothing as a sort 10.55.50 D – you have – creating the impression you are medical doctor A – no I never did VO: The HPCSA would disagree. Dr Jeewa admits the centre has not been registered since 2003 – he blames government procedures and says he was never told to close. D – this operation was operating illegally A – yes correct BROOKE: Dr Anwar Jeewa // was so promising that he could cure my husband // come to this beautiful clinic, I’ll take care of you, you’ll have a nurse bedside 24 hours, a heart monitor // it was like he was promoting it no different than staying in a hospital // INT1 M7 VO: This is CCTV footage of the night Milos died – there were three other patients and only one nurse on duty, no medical doctor. D – doc on premisies A – nno… 10.20.38 D- 24 support A – medicial D – you A – all do it D – doesn’t make it right. DR MASH: Everything, everything is wrong with that. You can’t, you can not – ibogaine has a very narrow therapeutic to toxic margin – you can not give ibogaine without a medical doctor present – // CUT // you can not be giving ibogaine if you are not having a patient being monitored with cardiac screening. INT1 M22 VO: Look carefully, you’ll see that Milos is not connected to the ECG machine, let alone someone monitoring it. 10.30.00 A – were you equipped to handle the er D – wasn’t hooked up A – allright ok VO: But for the family, it’s definitely not ok – it’s a neglect of duty. metadata.Summary: Ibogaine is a highly controversial drug only available in 7 countries – South Africa is one of them. Intended to treat opiod addiction, but not recommended for benzodiazepines. A Canadian citizen came to SA to get off his anti-depressant addiction. He arrived and died two days later at a rehab centre run by not a doctor but a dentist. The family fears that the South African legal system will fail serve justice for what they say is the murder of Milos Martinovic. We get exclusive interviews with his wife and father – both broken by his loss, angry at charlatan dentist and deeply concerned about the rule of law in the country.
